description: A perennial woody climber that grips supports with aerial roots and grows 4-6 m tall, with glossy, dark green, broadly ovate leaves. Hanging spikes of tiny flowers produce small round berries that turn from green to red; dried unripe berries become black peppercorns.
cultural_significance: Called 'black gold', pepper drove the ancient spice trade from the Malabar Coast. It is a member of Trikatu and a daily kitchen spice. Pippali (long pepper) is the Vedic-era pepper, while Maricha is better known in later texts.
habitat: Humid tropical forests; cultivated on support trees such as coconut, arecanut and silver oak on the Malabar Coast and the Western Ghats.

uses.title: Cough, cold and sore throat
uses.detail: Maricha with honey, tulsi or ginger is a classic household preparation described as Kaphahara.

uses.title: Poor digestion and loss of appetite
uses.detail: As part of Trikatu (ginger, black pepper, long pepper) it is traditionally used to kindle digestive fire (Deepana).

uses.title: Fever and congestion
uses.detail: Pepper decoctions with tulsi and ginger are traditionally used in seasonal fevers.

uses.title: Bioavailability enhancement
uses.detail: Piperine is studied for improving absorption of some compounds such as curcumin; it can also affect drug metabolism.

uses.title: Sinus and headache relief (inhalation or paste)
uses.detail: Traditional folk use as a stimulant of nasal secretions; use with caution.

ayurveda.vedic_note: Not a Vedic-era plant by name; the Vedic and early texts refer to Pippali (long pepper), while Maricha rises to prominence in later Ayurvedic texts and trade.

preparations.name: Maricha churna (powder)
preparations.note: Used in Trikatu and many classical formulae.

preparations.name: Trikatu churna
preparations.method: Mix equal parts dried ginger, black pepper and long pepper.
preparations.note: A classical digestive and respiratory formulation.

preparations.name: Pepper kwatha (decoction)
preparations.method: Boil crushed peppercorns with tulsi and ginger.

preparations.name: Pepper-honey mixture
preparations.method: Mix a pinch of fine powder with honey.

precautions: Large amounts can irritate the stomach and aggravate ulcers, acidity or piles. Piperine can alter the way the body processes some medicines (for example phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline), so consult a doctor on regular medicines. Use only food amounts in pregnancy. Inhaling the powder can trigger sneezing and coughing.

cultivation.climate: Hot, humid tropical; 23-32 C with 2000+ mm rain
cultivation.water: High; consistent moisture but no waterlogging
cultivation.propagation: Rooted stem cuttings planted at the foot of a support tree in the monsoon
cultivation.harvest: Pick when one or two berries on a spike turn red; sun-dry for black pepper

conservation_status: Not threatened; widely cultivated. Wild populations occur in the Western Ghats.
fun_fact: Black, white and green pepper all come from the same plant, differing only in when the berries are picked and how they are processed.

regions.name: Malabar Coast
regions.note: Historic centre of the pepper trade

regions.name: Thailand & Indochina
regions.note: Vietnam is the world's largest producer
